SOURCE ESSAY:
A naval gentleman of importance having asked me who the original Davy Jones was, I was rendered mute and ashamed. The shame ought properly to have been his, since he is in the Admiralty, where the secrets of the sea should be known, and is covered with buttons and gold braid; but there is caprice in these matters, and it is I (as a defaulting literary person) who felt it.

I left with bent head, determined, directly I reached London and books were again accessible, to find the answer. But have I found it? You shall decide.

I began with a "Glossary of Sea Terms," which is glib enough about the meaning of Davy Jones's locker but silent as to derivation. I passed on to "The Oxford Dictionary," there to find the meaning more precisely stated, after directions how to pronounce Davy's name. You or I would assume that he should be pronounced as he is spelt: just Davy; but the late Dr. Murray knew better. You don't say Davy; you say Dē.vi . Having invented and solved these difficulties, the Dictionary proceeds: "Nautical slang. The spirit of the sea, the sailor's devil. Davy Jones's locker: the ocean, the deep, especially as the grave of those who perish at sea." Among the authors cited is Smollett in "Peregrine Pickle," and also one J. Willock, to whom I shall return later.

Still on the search for an origin of Davy Jones I went next to "The Dictionary of National Biography" (which, if only you could get it ashore, is, no matter what the pundits say as to the Bible and Boswell and Plato and "The Golden Treasury," and so forth, the best book for a desert island), and there I found no fewer than eight David Joneses, all of course Welsh, not one of whom, however, could possibly claim any connexion with our hero; three being hymn-writers and antiquaries, one a revivalist, one a soldier and translator, one a barrister, one a missionary to Madagascar (the only one who knew anything of the sea), and one a mad preacher whose troubles caused his "coal-black hair to turn milk-white in a night"—as mine seemed likely soon to do. However, I then bethought me of what I should have done first, and seeking the shelves where "Notes and Queries" reside was at once rewarded. For "Notes and Queries" had tackled the problem and done with it as long ago as 1851. On June 14 of that year Mr. Henry Campkin requested the little paper (which, since Captain Cuttle provided it with its excellent motto, should have a certain friendliness towards nautical questions) to help him. Mr. Campkin, however, did not, as my Admiralty friend did, say, "By the way, who the devil was Davy Jones?" He asked, as a gentleman should, in gentlemanly, if precise, terms: "Who was the important individual whose name has become so powerful a myth? And what occasioned the identification of the ocean itself with the locker of this mysterious person?"

Mr. Campkin, who obviously should have occupied a seat in the House of Commons, was answered in record time, much quicker than would be his fortune to-day; for on June 21 Mr. Pemberton, the only reader of "Notes and Queries" ever to take up the challenge, made his reply, and with that reply our knowledge begins and ends. Mr. Pemberton said that being himself a seafarer and having given much consideration to the question, he had come at length to the conclusion that the name of Davy Jones was derived from the prophet Jonah (who, of course, was not Welsh at all but an Israelite). Jonah, if not exactly a sailor, had had his marine adventures, and in his prayer thus refers to them: "The waters compassed me about ... the depth closed me round about; the weeds were wrapped about my head," and so forth. The sea, then, Mr. Pemberton continued, "might not be misappropriately termed by a rude mariner Jonah's locker"; while Jonah would naturally soon be familiarised into Jones, and since all Joneses hail from the country from whose valleys and mountains Mr. Lloyd George derives his moving perorations, and since most Welshmen (Mr. Lloyd George being no exception) are named Davy, how natural that "Davy Jones" should emerge! That was Mr. Pemberton's theory, and the only one which I have discovered; but I am sure that Mrs. Gamp would support him—although she might prefer to substitute for the word "locker" the word which comic military poets always rhyme to "réveillé."

But, indeed, the more one thinks of it, the more reasonable does the story seem; for, as Mr. Pemberton might have gone on to say, there is further evidence for linking up Jonah and Jones in the genus of fish which swallowed the prophet but failed to retain him. To a dialectician of any parts the fatal association of whales and Wales would be child's play. Later I found that Dr. Brewer of "The Dictionary of Phrase and Fable" supports the Jonah theory whole-heartedly; but he goes on—to my mind very unnecessarily—to derive "Davy" from "duffy," a West Indian spirit. Thus, says he, Davy Jones's locker is really Duffy Jonah's locker—that is, the bottom of the sea, or the place where the sailors intended to consign Jonah. The confusion is rather comic. First, a man of God whom the crew throws overboard. Secondly a fish, divinely sent to save the man of God. Thirdly, the use of the man of God's name to signify the sailor's devil, with himself as sinister ruler of an element which he had the best reasons for hating. Thus do myths grow.

So much for Davy Jones. J. Willock, however, another of the authorities whom "The Oxford Dictionary" cites, plunges us into a further mystery. In one of his Voyages he says: "The great bugbear of the ocean is Davie Jones. At the crossing of the line they call out that Davie Jones and his wife are coming on board...."

"And his wife"!

But with the identity of Mrs. Davy Jones I refuse to concern myself—not even though the whole Board of Admiralty command it.

message.content:
A distinguished naval officer once posed a question to me regarding the origins of Davy Jones, leaving me speechless and embarrassed. The embarrassment should have belonged to him, given his position within the Admiralty, where knowledge of maritime lore is expected. However, the whims of circumstance found me, a mere literary figure, feeling the weight of that moment.

With my head bowed, I resolved that upon my return to London and access to books, I would uncover the truth. But have I truly discovered it? That is for you to determine.

I commenced my inquiry with a "Glossary of Sea Terms," which offered a slick explanation regarding Davy Jones's locker but failed to address its etymology. I then progressed to "The Oxford Dictionary," where the definition was presented with greater clarity, including guidance on the pronunciation of Davy’s name. Many might presume that it is pronounced as it appears—simply Davy—but the late Dr. Murray had a different perspective. The correct pronunciation is Dē.vi. After navigating this confusion, the Dictionary elaborated on nautical slang, defining Davy Jones as “the spirit of the sea, the sailor's devil,” and described Davy Jones’s locker as the ocean, particularly as a grave for those who meet their demise at sea. Among the references was Smollett’s "Peregrine Pickle," along with one J. Willock, whom I will revisit later.

Determined to trace the origin of Davy Jones, I turned to "The Dictionary of National Biography," which, despite its limitations in being unavailable for casual reading ashore, remains an invaluable resource—arguably more essential than the Bible or works by Boswell, Plato, and others, should one find themselves stranded on a desert island. To my surprise, I discovered eight individuals named David Jones, all of Welsh descent; yet none could be directly linked to the legendary figure in question. Among them were hymn-writers, a revivalist, a soldier and translator, a barrister, a missionary to Madagascar (the only one with any maritime experience), and a fervent preacher whose life challenges turned his hair from coal-black to white overnight—an eventuality mine seemed destined to follow. 

Reflecting on my approach, it occurred to me that I should have consulted "Notes and Queries" first, where I was promptly rewarded. This publication had addressed the very question back in 1851. On June 14, that year, a Mr. Henry Campkin sought assistance from the periodical, which, given its nautical motto courtesy of Captain Cuttle, should have welcomed inquiries of this nature. Unlike my Admiralty acquaintance, Mr. Campkin did not bluntly inquire, "Who the devil was Davy Jones?" Instead, he posed the question in a gentlemanly fashion, asking, "Who was the significant individual whose name has become such a powerful myth? And what led to the ocean being identified with the locker of this enigmatic figure?"

Mr. Campkin's request was answered remarkably quickly—much faster than one might expect today. By June 21, Mr. Pemberton, the only reader of "Notes and Queries" to rise to the occasion, provided an answer that would serve as a cornerstone for our understanding. As a seafarer himself, Mr. Pemberton had pondered the question at length and proposed that the name Davy Jones might have originated from the biblical prophet Jonah (who, notably, was not Welsh but an Israelite). While Jonah was not precisely a sailor, his own seafaring exploits are well-documented; in his prayer, he reflects upon his experiences with the ocean: "The waters compassed me about... the depth closed me round about; the weeds were wrapped about my head," and so forth. Thus, Pemberton posited, the sea might be fittingly referred to as Jonah's locker by an unrefined mariner, and the name Jonah could naturally have morphed into Jones. Given that many Welshmen (including Mr. Lloyd George, from whom we derive stirring oratory) are often named Davy, it follows that "Davy Jones" would eventually emerge. This theory from Mr. Pemberton appears to be the sole explanation I have encountered, though I suspect Mrs. Gamp might lend her support—albeit with a humorous twist, preferring a different term for "locker" that comic military poets often rhyme with "réveillé."

The more one contemplates this theory, the more plausible it becomes. As Mr. Pemberton might have elaborated, there is further evidence linking Jonah and Jones through the fish that swallowed the prophet but subsequently did not retain him. For a skilled dialectician, the connection between whales and Wales would present no challenge. Later, I discovered that Dr. Brewer, in "The Dictionary of Phrase and Fable," fervently endorses the Jonah connection, but he unnecessarily posits that "Davy" derives from "duffy," a spirit from the West Indies. Thus, according to his interpretation, Davy Jones's locker becomes Duffy Jonah's locker—essentially the seabed, or the place where sailors intended to send Jonah. The resulting confusion is rather comical: first, a man of God cast overboard by the crew; second, a divine fish sent to rescue him; and third, the misuse of the prophet’s name to denote the sailor’s devil, with Jonah becoming an unwitting ruler of the very element he had reason to despise. This is how myths take shape.

And so much for Davy Jones. Yet, J. Willock, another author referenced by "The Oxford Dictionary," leads us into yet another enigma. In one of his voyages, he mentions: "The great bugbear of the ocean is Davie Jones. At the crossing of the line, they shout that Davie Jones and his wife are coming aboard...."

"And his wife!"

As for the identity of Mrs. Davy Jones, I shall refrain from delving into that mystery—regardless of any orders from the Board of Admiralty.
